claims.text: The primary sector consists of businesses that extract or harvest raw materials from natural resources. Mining, farming, fishing, forestry and quarrying belong to it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The secondary sector consists of businesses that process raw materials or components into finished or part-finished goods. Manufacturing, food processing, assembly and construction belong to it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The tertiary sector consists of businesses that provide services rather than physical output, to consumers or to other businesses. Retailing, transport, banking, insurance, tourism, education and health care belong to it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The quaternary sector consists of knowledge-based activity: research and development, information services, data processing, consultancy and software development. It is a part of service activity that some classifications separate out because the output is knowledge rather than a service delivered to a customer on the spot.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A sector describes an activity, not a company, so one business may operate in more than one sector at once. A firm that catches hake, freezes and cans it, and sells it through its own shops is carrying out primary, secondary and tertiary activity, and a question about its sector has to say which of its activities is being classified.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: In Namibia, mining and fishing are the largest primary activities, fish and meat processing and beverage production are the main secondary activities, and tourism, retailing, transport, banking and government services make up most tertiary activity. Quaternary activity is small but growing, in geological survey work, software and telecommunications.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The private sector consists of businesses owned and controlled by private individuals or by other private organisations. Their objectives are set by their owners, and profit is usually among them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The public sector consists of organisations owned and controlled by the state on behalf of the population. They are funded mainly from taxation and government borrowing, their objectives are set by government, and any surplus belongs to the state.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The two sectors are usually separated by who owns the organisation and by what it is for. A private-sector business answers to owners who have put their own money in, so profit, growth and return tend to dominate its objectives. A public-sector organisation answers to government, so access, coverage and the price paid by users tend to dominate, and it may be kept running in places or at prices where a commercial operator would make a loss.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The line between the sectors is not always sharp. A state-owned enterprise is owned by government but trades commercially and may be expected to cover its costs; a public-private partnership has a private firm build or run a facility under a government contract. Both are mixtures, and which sector they are counted in depends on who holds ownership and control.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The public sector and a public limited company are different things and the shared word causes a great deal of lost credit. A public limited company is privately owned, by its shareholders, and sits in the private sector. The word public in its name refers to the fact that its shares may be offered to the general public, not to state ownership.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The relative importance of a sector is its share of national output or of total employment, so the figure is a proportion rather than a total. A sector can therefore fall in relative importance while its output is still rising, because the rest of the economy is growing faster.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The share of output and employment held by the primary sector tends to fall as a country's income per head rises. Mechanisation raises output for each worker employed, so the same tonnage needs fewer people; reserves of a mineral are depleted and extraction becomes dearer; and households spending extra income spend proportionally less of it on food and raw materials and more on services.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The secondary sector tends to grow in relative importance during industrialisation. Investment in plant, transferred technology, a supply of labour at wages below those of established manufacturing countries, and government support through infrastructure or protection all raise the return on manufacturing inside the country, which draws capital and workers into it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Deindustrialisation is a fall in the share of output and employment held by the secondary sector in an economy where manufacturing was already established. It is driven by competition from producers whose costs are lower, by domestic wages rising faster than productivity, by firms relocating production abroad, and by demand shifting towards services as incomes rise.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The tertiary and quaternary sectors tend to grow in relative importance as incomes rise, because spending on services such as travel, health care, finance and entertainment rises more than proportionally with income. Two further forces add to it: communications technology makes services tradeable over distance, and manufacturers contract out activities such as cleaning, logistics and information technology that were once counted inside the secondary sector.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The main cost of a sector shift falls on workers whose skills were specific to the declining sector. A rock-drill operator whose mine closes does not become a software developer, so the jobs created in a growing sector may not be open to the people the shrinking sector released. The result is structural unemployment, and because extraction and heavy manufacturing are concentrated in particular towns, the loss is concentrated there too while the new jobs appear elsewhere.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: For an individual business a sector shift changes four things it has to plan around: where its customers' spending is going, how easily it can recruit the skills it needs and what it has to pay for them, what its suppliers can still supply locally, and where government attention and support are directed. A supplier of drilling consumables to a shrinking mining sector faces falling orders whatever it does well.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The types of business ownership differ on four things, and almost every advantage and disadvantage in this topic comes back to one of them: who owns the business, whether the business has a legal identity separate from its owners, who is liable for its debts, and which ways of raising capital the form allows.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: An unincorporated business has no legal identity separate from its owners. The owners make the contracts personally and carry unlimited liability, and the business ends in law when they leave it. An incorporated business is a separate legal person: it owns assets, makes contracts, sues and is sued in its own name, its members have limited liability, and it continues to exist when a member sells out or dies. Sole traders and ordinary partnerships are unincorporated; private limited companies and public limited companies are incorporated.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Four of the eight types the syllabus names are legal forms of ownership in themselves: sole trader, partnership, private limited company and public limited company. The other four describe how a business is run or what it exists for, and each is carried inside one of those legal forms. A franchise is a trading agreement, a joint venture is an agreement between businesses, a co-operative is a way of dividing ownership and votes among members, and a social enterprise is defined by its purpose. Naming the legal form and naming the arrangement are two separate answers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The choice of ownership is not permanent. A business may move from one form to another as it grows or as its owners' circumstances change, and the move costs money, time and paperwork, so it is a decision in its own right rather than an automatic consequence of getting bigger.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A sole trader is a business owned and controlled by one person, who provides the capital, keeps the profit after tax and is personally liable for the debts. The business is unincorporated, so in law the owner and the business are the same person.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The sole trader form is the quickest and cheapest to start, because it needs no registration of a separate legal person and, beyond any trading licence the activity itself requires, little formal paperwork. The owner takes every decision without consulting anyone, keeps all of the profit, and does not have to publish accounts, so competitors cannot read the figures.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Four things limit the sole trader form. Liability is unlimited, so personal assets are exposed. Capital is restricted to what the owner can put in or borrow, because the form has no shares to sell. The business has no continuity in law: if the owner dies or stops trading, it ends, and the assets pass through the estate. And one person carries every function, so illness stops the business and skills the owner lacks have to be bought in or done badly.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The word sole in sole trader refers to ownership, not to the number of people working there. A sole trader may employ staff, and many do; what makes the business a sole trader is that one person owns and controls it and carries the liability alone.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A partnership is a business owned by two or more people who share the capital, the profits and the control of it. An ordinary partnership is unincorporated, so the partners carry unlimited liability for the debts of the business. Many jurisdictions set an upper limit on the number of partners, commonly twenty, with exceptions for professions such as accountancy and law.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A partnership agreement, sometimes called a deed of partnership, is the written contract between the partners. It normally sets out how much capital each partner contributes, how profits and losses are divided, what each partner's role and authority is, how decisions are taken, and how a partner may be admitted or may leave. Where there is no agreement, the default rules of the jurisdiction apply instead, and those rules may divide profit equally however unequal the contributions were.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Against a sole trader, a partnership brings in more capital, more skills and someone to share the workload and the decisions with, and it lets the partners specialise. Against that, the profit is divided, decisions have to be agreed so the business moves more slowly, and each partner can bind the others: an ordinary partner's contracts and debts are the responsibility of all the partners, so one partner's mistake reaches the personal assets of the rest.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Many jurisdictions allow a sleeping partner, who contributes capital and shares profit but takes no part in running the business, and some allow a limited partner whose liability is capped at the amount contributed provided that partner does not manage the business. Whether either form is available, and on what terms, depends on the law of the country the partnership is registered in.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A private limited company is an incorporated business owned by shareholders whose shares are issued privately to people the company chooses. Its shares may not be offered for sale to the general public. It is a separate legal person from its shareholders, and their liability is limited.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Incorporating as a private limited company gives the shareholders limited liability, gives the business continuity that does not depend on any one owner, and opens routes to capital that an unincorporated business does not have, because shares can be issued to new investors. Because those shares go to people the existing shareholders agree to admit, control stays within a known group, which is why the form suits a family business that wants outside money without outside command.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The costs of the private limited company form are formation expense and legal formality, an obligation to file accounts and details of directors that are then open to inspection, and the loss of privacy that goes with it. Shares are also hard to sell, because there is no public market for them and the other shareholders commonly have to approve a transfer, so a shareholder who wants out may wait a long time for a buyer.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Directors run a private limited company on the shareholders' behalf, and in a small company the same people are usually both. Where they are the same people, incorporation changes the legal position without changing who actually decides anything from day to day.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A public limited company is an incorporated business whose shares may be offered for sale to the general public, and are commonly traded on a stock exchange. Its shareholders have limited liability, it is a separate legal person, and company law sets a minimum share capital and fuller disclosure requirements than for a private limited company.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Flotation, also called an initial public offering, is the process by which a company becomes a public limited company and offers its shares to the general public for the first time. It puts sums of capital within reach that the other forms of ownership do not provide, and it gives existing shareholders a market on which they can sell part of their holding.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The costs of the public limited company form are substantial. Flotation itself carries legal, accounting, underwriting and marketing fees; the company must publish full accounts and announce information that competitors can read; ownership is dispersed among many shareholders, so no founder holds the same authority as before; anyone may buy the shares, so the company is exposed to an unwanted takeover; and shareholders who can sell at any time tend to press for results in the current year.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Divorce of ownership and control is the separation, in a company with many shareholders, between the people who own it and the directors who run it. Shareholders own the company but do not manage it, and directors manage it without owning much of it, so the two groups' interests may diverge: directors may pursue growth, prestige or their own security where shareholders want dividends and a rising share price.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A franchise is an agreement under which one business, the franchisor, grants another, the franchisee, the right to trade under its brand name and to use its business format in a defined area. In return the franchisee normally pays an initial fee and a continuing royalty, commonly a percentage of sales revenue, and agrees to run the outlet the franchisor's way.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: For the franchisee the attraction is that the format has already been tested, so the risk of failure is lower than starting an unknown business from nothing, and the brand brings customers from the first day, along with training, a supply chain and national advertising the franchisee could not pay for alone. The price is a permanent share of revenue, a share that is payable whether the outlet is profitable or not, and the loss of freedom over what is sold, how it is priced and how the outlet looks. Selling the business on usually requires the franchisor's consent.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: For the franchisor the attraction is expansion financed by other people's capital and run by owner-operators with their own money at stake, which tends to produce more care than a salaried manager gives, plus a royalty income that grows with the network. The price is weaker direct control: quality depends on people the franchisor does not employ, and one franchisee's poor hygiene or rudeness damages the brand everywhere.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A franchise is a contract, not a legal form of ownership. The franchisee still has to be something in law, and is commonly a sole trader or a private limited company, so the liability the franchisee carries is decided by that choice and not by the franchise agreement.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A co-operative is a business owned and democratically controlled by its members, who are the people who use it: its workers, the producers who supply it, or the customers who buy from it. Voting is normally one member one vote, whatever each member has contributed, and the surplus is shared among members in proportion to their use of the business rather than to their capital.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Three kinds of co-operative are common. A worker co-operative is owned by the people employed in it. A producer co-operative is owned by producers who pool processing, transport or marketing, which is the usual form in agriculture: communal farmers who market cattle together, or a marula oil group that presses and sells jointly. A consumer or retail co-operative is owned by the customers who shop in it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The strength of the co-operative form is bargaining power and shared cost: members who could not afford storage, transport or a buyer relationship on their own can afford them together, and members who own the business have a reason to support it. The weaknesses follow from the same structure. One member one vote makes decisions slow and makes it hard to reward a member who puts in more capital, so capital is scarce, and a business run by its members may lack specialist management unless it pays to bring some in.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A joint venture is an agreement between two or more businesses to pool resources for a particular project or to form a jointly owned business, sharing the cost, the risk, the control and the returns. The businesses stay separate and independent in everything outside the venture.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Businesses form joint ventures to get something the partner already has and they would take years to build: local knowledge of a market, an established distribution network, a technology or a licence, or a permit that a foreign firm cannot obtain alone. A joint venture also splits the cost and the risk of a project too large or too uncertain for one firm, and in some countries a partnership with a local business is a condition of being allowed to operate at all.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Joint ventures fail for predictable reasons: the partners want different things from the venture, one contributes less than it promised, management styles and decision-making cultures clash, and profits and responsibility are argued over. There is also a longer risk, that a partner learns the technology or the market during the venture and later uses it to compete.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A social enterprise is a business that earns its revenue by trading, but whose primary objective is a social or environmental purpose rather than a return to owners. Most or all of its surplus is reinvested in that purpose instead of being distributed as profit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Social enterprises are often described as working to a triple bottom line: they measure themselves on economic performance, on social benefit such as employment, training or access to a service, and on environmental effect. Performance against all three is reported, which is what separates the form from a conventional business that gives some of its profit away.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A social enterprise is defined by its purpose and by what happens to its surplus, not by one legal form. It may be registered as a private limited company, as a co-operative or as a trust, and it is distinct both from a charity, which does not principally trade for its income, and from a conventional business that supports a good cause out of profit it otherwise keeps.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The advantage of the social enterprise form is that the purpose is built into the business rather than depending on donations, and that purpose attracts committed staff, customers who prefer to buy from it, and grant funding a conventional firm could not apply for. The difficulty is the same purpose pulling against survival: prices are held down for the people the enterprise exists to serve, surplus is reinvested rather than paid out, and investors seeking a financial return have little reason to put money in, so capital is harder to raise than for a comparable commercial business.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Which form of ownership suits a business is decided by a small number of questions: how much capital it needs and how soon, how much personal risk the owners are willing to carry, how much control they want to keep, what their objectives are, how fast they intend to grow, how much set-up cost and formality they can carry, and whether the activity itself is one the law requires to be conducted in a particular form.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Capital need and control pull against each other. Raising more money from outside usually means admitting someone who then has a claim on profit and a say in decisions: a partner brings capital in exchange for a share of profit and of control, a new shareholder in a private limited company takes both, and a flotation spreads them among thousands of people. An owner who will not give up control is therefore choosing to be limited to what can be borrowed or retained.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The value of limited liability rises with what the owner has to lose and with how risky the trade is. A consultant working from home with few debts risks little by remaining a sole trader; a builder who signs contracts worth many times the value of the business, and who owns a house, is exposed to a loss that could take everything, so incorporation is worth its cost to that owner and may not be to the first.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: There is no form of ownership that suits every business. Appropriateness is judged against one business's own circumstances and objectives, and the answer may change as those change, which is why a form that was right at the start can be the wrong one five years later.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Size and legal form are separate things. Some private limited companies employ thousands of people and some public limited companies are small, so a business cannot be classified by its turnover or its headcount. What decides the form is how the business is owned, not how big it is.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Unlimited liability means the owner and the business are the same in law, so the owner is personally responsible for the debts of the business without any limit. If the business cannot pay, the owner's personal assets, including a house, a vehicle or savings, may be sold to settle what is owed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Limited liability means a shareholder's responsibility for the company's debts is limited to the amount that shareholder has agreed to pay for the shares. The company is a separate legal person, so the debt belongs to the company; a shareholder who has paid for the shares in full stands to lose that investment and no more of their personal wealth.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The difference between the two comes from incorporation and nothing else. Registering a company creates a legal person separate from the people who own it, and it is that separation that puts the debt on the company rather than on the owners. Where there is no separate legal person there is no limit on liability, which is why sole traders and ordinary partners carry it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Limited liability matters to owners because it caps the downside of a venture before it starts. A person who knows that failure costs the money invested, and not the family home, will take on a project they would otherwise refuse, and outside investors will put money into a business whose management they cannot supervise. More capital reaches new and risky ventures as a result than would reach them if every shareholder were liable for everything.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Limited liability shifts risk onto the people the company owes money to, because their claim stops at the company's own assets. Lenders and suppliers respond to that: a bank asked to lend to a small company with few assets may require security over property or a personal guarantee from the directors, and a supplier may ask for payment in advance until a trading record exists. Where a director signs a personal guarantee, the protection of limited liability is given up for that particular debt.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Limited liability is not a shield against every personal consequence. It does not cover a debt a director has personally guaranteed, and company law in most jurisdictions allows a director to be held personally responsible where a company was allowed to go on trading and taking on debts once there was no reasonable prospect of paying them. The precise rules and the thresholds that trigger them depend on the jurisdiction.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Four changes of ownership form are common. A sole trader takes in a partner and becomes a partnership. A sole trader or a partnership incorporates and becomes a private limited company. A private limited company floats and becomes a public limited company. And a public limited company returns to private status by buying its shares back from the general public.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Incorporating brings limited liability, continuity independent of any one owner, the ability to issue shares, and often a firmer standing with suppliers and lenders who can inspect filed accounts. It costs formation and continuing compliance expense, the publication of accounts that competitors and customers can read, more administration than the owner did before, and a share of future profits wherever new shareholders are admitted.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Flotation brings capital on a scale the other forms do not reach, a tradeable share that lets founders realise part of what they have built, and public profile. It costs the expense of the issue itself, full disclosure of results, the dilution of the founders' control, exposure to a takeover once anyone may buy the shares, and pressure from shareholders for results in the current year rather than in five years' time.

claims.text: Dilution is the arithmetic behind the loss of control. Issuing new shares raises the total number in issue, so a founder whose holding does not change owns a smaller proportion of the company than before, and receives a smaller proportion of any dividend. Once the founder's holding falls below half of the votes, decisions can be carried against the founder, and below the level company law sets for special resolutions the founder can no longer block a change to the company's constitution.

claims.text: Changes of form are made in both directions. A public limited company may buy its shares back and return to private status to escape the cost of disclosure, the pressure for short-term results and the threat of a takeover, accepting in exchange that raising large sums quickly becomes harder again.

claims.text: A change of ownership form is worth making when what it brings in is worth more to the owners than what it takes away, judged against their own objectives. Capital and protection from liability are bought with control, privacy, cost and a share of profit, so the same change can be right for a business that needs capital urgently and wrong for one whose owners value independence more than growth.
